rulers.title: The two rulers, at every size
rulers.caption: The two rulers of [Is a world a space?](how-many-dimensions-does-a-world-have.md#two-rulers) on B1's worlds that are not stars, each line the median of the worlds of one size. From dark to bright: Experiment 8's worlds of 12,800 to 409,600 tokens (two or three of each size; below 12,800 tokens most of its worlds are stars). Grey: the 16 worlds of 10,000 tokens of Experiment 2 (dotted) and the 23 of 100,000 tokens of Experiment 10 (dashed). Left: the local dimension from balls, until a typical ball holds a quarter of its world, over the worlds and five moments of their settled lives. Right: the spectral dimension from a lazy random walk after their last game, of up to 1,024 steps, and of up to 8,192 in the worlds of 409,600 tokens, until it is back no more than 5/n more often than at rest.
rulers.recipe:
**Runs.** The 25 baseline worlds of Experiment 8 that lived to iteration 600 — B1 at 1,600 to 409,600 tokens, seeds 1 to 3, of which one world of 1,600 tokens and all of 3,200 tokens and more (`B1-1600-s002`, `B1-3200-s001` … `B1-409600-s003`; [Worlds of many sizes](how-does-a-worlds-size-follow-its-tokens.md); `python3 gol_lab.py run E08`), after the game of iteration 599. The 26 baseline worlds that lived to the end (`B1-10000-s001` … `-s030`, [The life of a B1 world](a-worlds-life.md); `python3 gol_lab.py run E02`). The 30 baseline worlds that lived to the end (`B1-100000-s001` … `-s030`, [Worlds of many sizes](how-does-a-worlds-size-follow-its-tokens.md); `python3 gol_lab.py run E10`).

**Data.** From each run's frames, `GraphOfLifeRuns/<run>/frames/`, read with `gol_store.read_frame(run, index)`; frame `2·t` is iteration *t* after reproduction and frame `2·t + 1` after the game.

1. Read the frame after each world's last game; build its network from `edges` and keep its largest piece (`book_chapters.space.largest_piece`). Its random twin: the same numbers of links per agent wired at random (`book_graph.degree_preserving`, seed 23), its largest piece.
2. Balls: a breadth-first search all the way out from each of 100 agents drawn at random (seed 23); N(r) the geometric mean of the numbers within r steps; d(r) = ln(N(r+1)/N(r)) / ln((r+1)/r), read while N(r+1) is less than a quarter of the piece (`book_chapters.scaledims.reach` and `ball_curve`).
3. Walks: a lazy random walk (stay with probability ½, else step to a neighbour drawn at random) from each of 48 agents drawn at random, its distribution propagated exactly, for up to 1,024 steps; P(t) the probability of being back at the start minus that of being there at rest (the walk is reversible, so the chance to be back after 2m steps follows from where it is after m, and half the steps are propagated); d(t) = −2 · ln(P(2t)/P(t)) / ln 2 on a grid of t of ratio √2, read while P(2t) is above 5/n (`walk` and `walk_curve`).
4. A world whose best-linked agent was joined, on average over iterations 500 to its end, to a tenth of its agents or more is a star ([Stars and hubs](stars-and-hubs.md); `maxDegree`/`nodes` of its rows in `stats.jsonl`).
5. The same balls, of each world and of its twin, after the games of five iterations evenly spaced over its settled life, from 500 to its last (500, 525, 550, 574 and 599 in Experiment 8; 500, 750, 1,000, 1,249 and 1,499 in Experiment 10; 500, 1,125, 1,750, 2,374 and 2,999 in Experiment 2); each reading the median of the five (`book_chapters.scaledims.settled`).
6. In the three worlds of 409,600 tokens, the same 48 walks for up to 8,192 steps (`book_chapters.scaledims.long_reading`).
7. Each line: at every radius (or walk), the median over the worlds of that size (and, for the balls, their five moments) that read there, where at least half of them do.

**To make it again:** `python3 book_figures.py scaledims`.

bodies.title: What an edge does to the rulers
bodies.caption: Bodies whose dimension is known and which end at an edge, as a world does: a disc cut out of a square grid (dimension 2) and a ball cut out of a cubic grid (dimension 3), of 250, 500, 1,000 … 64,000 points, each twice the last, from dark to bright, read by the same code as the worlds. Top: the local dimension from balls, until a typical ball holds a quarter of the body; dashed, the same grid with no edge at all, counted exactly. Bottom: the spectral dimension from a lazy random walk of up to 1,024 steps.
bodies.recipe:
**Runs.** No runs: the bodies are built by `book_chapters.scaledims.body`.

**Data.** From the bodies themselves.

1. Bodies: the n points of a square or cubic grid nearest its centre (and any as near as the last), each linked to the points beside it that are inside too (`book_chapters.scaledims.body`), for n = 250, 500, … 64,000; read as the worlds are. The endless grids' balls are counted exactly: Σₖ 2ᵏ·C(d, k)·C(r, k) points within r steps.
2. Balls and walks as for the worlds: 100 balls grown all the way out and 48 walks of up to 1,024 steps, from points drawn at random (seed 23).

**To make it again:** `python3 book_figures.py scaledims`.

fixed.title: One radius, every size
fixed.caption: The local dimension from balls, read between the same two radii at every size, against the agents of a world's largest piece (logarithmic). Each dot is a world, its median over five moments of its settled life: blue, Experiment 8's worlds of 1,600 to 409,600 tokens; green, Experiment 2's worlds of 10,000 tokens; yellow, Experiment 10's of 100,000 tokens; grey, the stars among them. A world whose typical ball holds a quarter of it before the outer radius, at most of its moments, has no dot. Lines, read the same way at 250 to 64,000 points: red, the ball cut out of a cubic grid; violet, the disc cut out of a square grid. Dashed: the same grids with no edge.

width.title: How wide a world is, at every size
width.caption: The typical distance of each world — the number of steps within which a typical agent's ball holds half of the world's largest piece — against the agents in that piece, both the medians over five moments of its settled life, on logarithmic axes. Blue: Experiment 8's worlds of 1,600 to 409,600 tokens, and dashed, the power law fitted to those of 3,200 tokens and more that are not stars, agents^0.20 (95% interval 0.15 to 0.27); green: Experiment 2's of 10,000 tokens; yellow: Experiment 10's of 100,000 tokens; grey: the stars among them; orange: the random twins of the worlds that are not stars. Lines: the disc and the ball cut out of a grid. On these axes a body of d dimensions is a line of slope 1/d, and a random network a curve that flattens.
width.recipe:
**Runs.** The 25 baseline worlds of Experiment 8 that lived to iteration 600 — B1 at 1,600 to 409,600 tokens, seeds 1 to 3, of which one world of 1,600 tokens and all of 3,200 tokens and more (`B1-1600-s002`, `B1-3200-s001` … `B1-409600-s003`; [Worlds of many sizes](how-does-a-worlds-size-follow-its-tokens.md); `python3 gol_lab.py run E08`), after the game of iteration 599. 4. The same balls, of each world and of its twin, after the games of five iterations evenly spaced over its settled life, from 500 to its last (500, 525, 550, 574 and 599 in Experiment 8; 500, 750, 1,000, 1,249 and 1,499 in Experiment 10; 500, 1,125, 1,750, 2,374 and 2,999 in Experiment 2); each reading the median of the five (`book_chapters.scaledims.settled`).

7. Fit log₁₀(typical distance) = log₁₀ a + b · log₁₀(agents) by least squares over Experiment 8's worlds of 3,200 tokens and more that are not stars; the interval of b from 10,000 resamplings of the worlds within each size (`gol_analysis.power_fit`).

round3.title: Round 3's worlds, beside B1's at their size
round3.caption: The width of a world — its typical distance over its random twin's — against its agents, on logarithmic axes. Blue: B1's worlds that are not stars, each the median over five moments of its settled life, and dashed, the power law fitted to them. Green and orange: the worlds of round 3 of the [screen of random worlds](a-screen-of-random-worlds.md) that lived to the end of their runs, each averaged from iteration 100 on as [Which worlds are healthy?](which-worlds-are-healthy.md) reads them, by whether their dead are mended (`mend_on_death`).
round3.recipe:
**Runs.** The 25 baseline worlds of Experiment 8 that lived to iteration 600 — B1 at 1,600 to 409,600 tokens, seeds 1 to 3, of which one world of 1,600 tokens and all of 3,200 tokens and more (`B1-1600-s002`, `B1-3200-s001` … `B1-409600-s003`; [Worlds of many sizes](how-does-a-worlds-size-follow-its-tokens.md); `python3 gol_lab.py run E08`), after the game of iteration 599. Round 3 of the screen: every world of Experiments 40 to 42 that lived to the end of its run, 30,000 tokens, 3,000 iterations.

**Data.** From B1's frames, as above, and for round 3 `research/screen/health.json` (made by `research/screen/health.py` from the screen's readings).

1. Read the frame after each world's last game; build its network from `edges` and keep its largest piece (`book_chapters.space.largest_piece`). Its random twin: the same numbers of links per agent wired at random (`book_graph.degree_preserving`, seed 23), its largest piece.
2. Balls: a breadth-first search all the way out from each of 100 agents drawn at random (seed 23); N(r) the geometric mean of the numbers within r steps; d(r) = ln(N(r+1)/N(r)) / ln((r+1)/r), read while N(r+1) is less than a quarter of the piece (`book_chapters.scaledims.reach` and `ball_curve`).
3. A world whose best-linked agent was joined, on average over iterations 500 to its end, to a tenth of its agents or more is a star ([Stars and hubs](stars-and-hubs.md); `maxDegree`/`nodes` of its rows in `stats.jsonl`).
4. The same balls, of each world and of its twin, after the games of five iterations evenly spaced over its settled life, from 500 to its last (500, 525, 550, 574 and 599 in Experiment 8; 500, 750, 1,000, 1,249 and 1,499 in Experiment 10; 500, 1,125, 1,750, 2,374 and 2,999 in Experiment 2); each reading the median of the five (`book_chapters.scaledims.settled`).
5. Width: the typical distance over the twin's, at each moment; its median over the five. Fit log width against log agents over B1's worlds that are not stars (`gol_analysis.power_fit`).
6. Round 3: each world's `averages.width` and `averages.agents` in `health.json`, and `set.mend_on_death`; nothing is measured again.

**To make it again:** `python3 book_figures.py scaledims`.
